questions.question_text:
Which equation matches the graph shown?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=6.8cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-3.6,xmax=3.6,ymin=-1.5,ymax=12.5,xtick={-3,-2,-1,1,2,3},ytick={3,6,9,12},yticklabels={,6,9,12},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-3:3,samples=80]{x*x+3};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=1.5pt,black] coordinates {(0,3) (3,12)};\node[anchor=east,font=\small,xshift=-3pt] at (axis cs:0,3) {$3$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Changed the sign of the constant, placing the lowest point at $(0,-3)$ instead of $(0,3)$.
Used a negative coefficient, which makes the parabola open downward instead of upward.
Read the squared term as $2x$, giving a straight line instead of a parabola.

questions.solution_text:
The graph is a parabola opening upward with its lowest point at $(0,3)$.
The equation $y=x^{2}+3$ also gives $y=3^{2}+3=12$ at $x=3$, matching the plotted point $(3,12)$.

questions.question_text:
Which equation matches the graph shown?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=6.8cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-3.6,xmax=3.6,ymin=-1.5,ymax=11.5,xtick={-3,-2,-1,1,2,3},ytick={2,4,6,8,10},yticklabels={2,4,6,8,},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},xlabel style={at={(axis cs:3.6,0)},anchor=south west,xshift=6pt,yshift=3pt},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-3.3:3.3,samples=80]{-x*x+10};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=1.5pt,black] coordinates {(0,10) (3,1)};\node[anchor=south east,font=\small,xshift=-3pt,yshift=5pt] at (axis cs:0,10) {$10$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Dropped the negative sign on the squared term, making the parabola open upward.
Read $-x^{2}$ as $-2x$, giving a straight line instead of a parabola.

questions.solution_text:
The graph is a parabola opening downward with its highest point at $(0,10)$.
For $y=-x^{2}+10$, when $x=3$, $y=-9+10=1$, matching the plotted point $(3,1)$.

questions.question_text:
Which equation matches the graph shown? Check using the marked point.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=6.8cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-2.5,xmax=4.5,ymin=-1.5,ymax=18.5,xtick={-2,-1,1,2,3,4},ytick={4,8,12,16},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,red,<->,domain=-2.4:4.2,samples=80]{exp(x*ln(2))};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=1.5pt,black] coordinates {(4,16)};\node[anchor=south east,font=\small] at (axis cs:4,16) {$(4,16)$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Multiplied the base by $x$ instead of using a power; this gives a straight line and $y=8$ at $x=4$.
Changed the sign of the index, giving a decreasing curve and $y=\frac{1}{16}$ at $x=4$.

questions.solution_text:
The graph is an increasing exponential curve.
At the marked point, $2^{4}=16$, so $y=2^{x}$ matches $(4,16)$.

questions.question_text:
Which equation matches the graph shown? Check using the marked point.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=6.8cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-2.4,xmax=3.6,ymin=-1,ymax=10.5,xtick={-2,-1,1,2,3},ytick={1,3,6,9},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,red,<->,domain=-2.1:3.5,samples=80]{exp(-x*ln(3))};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=1.5pt,black] coordinates {(-2,9)};\node[anchor=south west,font=\small] at (axis cs:-2,9) {$(-2,9)$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Ignored the negative sign in the index, giving an increasing curve and $y=\frac{1}{9}$ at $x=-2$.
Put the negative sign outside the power, placing the curve below the $x$-axis.
Used base $2$ instead of $3$, giving $y=4$ rather than $9$ at $x=-2$.

questions.solution_text:
The graph decreases from left to right and stays above the $x$-axis.
At the marked point, $3^{-(-2)}=3^{2}=9$, so $y=3^{-x}$ matches $(-2,9)$.

questions.question_text:
The table shows the values of an exponential relationship.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ y & 2 & 6 & 18 & 54 \end{array}$
As $x$ increases by $1$, each $y$-value is:

options.why: Used the first gap $6-2=4$ as a constant difference, as for a straight line.
Read the starting value $2$ as the common ratio instead of dividing consecutive terms.
Found the correct ratio $3$ but described it as adding rather than multiplying.

questions.solution_text:
$6\div2=3$
$18\div6=3$
$54\div18=3$
Each $y$-value is multiplied by the common ratio $3$.

questions.question_text:
Which equation matches the graph shown?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=6.8cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-3.6,xmax=3.6,ymin=-5.5,ymax=6.5,xtick={-3,-2,-1,1,2,3},ytick={-4,-2,2,4,6},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-3.1:3.1,samples=80]{x*x-4};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=1.5pt,black] coordinates {(-2,0) (0,-4) (2,0)};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: A $+4$ constant would lift the lowest point to $(0,4)$, not $(0,-4)$.
A negative coefficient would make the parabola open downward, not upward.
An exponential curve has no turning point and never dips below the $x$-axis.

questions.solution_text:
The curve is a parabola opening **upward** with its lowest point at $(0,-4)$, so the constant is $-4$ and the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is positive.
$y=x^{2}-4$

questions.question_text:
Which equation matches the graph shown?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=6.8cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-3.6,xmax=3.6,ymin=-1.5,ymax=8.5,xtick={-3,-2,-1,1,2,3},ytick={2,4,6,8},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,red,<->,domain=-2.9:3.6,samples=60]{exp(-x*ln(2))};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=1.5pt,red] coordinates {(-2,4) (0,1) (2,0.25)};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: A growth curve rises from left to right; this curve falls, so the index is $-x$.
A parabola is symmetrical with a turning point; this curve has neither.
A reflected exponential lies below the $x$-axis; this curve stays above it.

questions.solution_text:
The curve falls from left to right, stays above the $x$-axis, and has no turning point, so it is an exponential **decay** curve.
$y=2^{-x}$

questions.question_text:
Which equation matches the graph shown?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=6.8cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-4.5,xmax=4.5,ymin=-1.5,ymax=10.5,xtick={-4,-3,-2,-1,1,2,3,4},xticklabels={-4,-3,-2,-1,1,2,3,},ytick={2,4,6,8,10},yticklabels={2,4,6,,10},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},xlabel style={at={(axis cs:4.5,0)},anchor=south west,xshift=8pt,yshift=3pt},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-4.2:4.2,samples=80]{-0.5*x*x+8};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=1.5pt,black] coordinates {(0,8) (2,6) (4,0)};\node[anchor=south east,font=\small,xshift=-3pt,yshift=5pt] at (axis cs:0,8) {$8$};\node[anchor=south west,font=\small,xshift=4pt,yshift=3pt] at (axis cs:4,0) {$4$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Dropped the factor $\frac{1}{2}$, giving $y=4$ instead of $6$ at $x=2$.
Dropped the negative sign, making the parabola open upward and giving $y=10$ at $x=2$.
Did not square $x$, giving a straight line and $y=7$ at $x=2$.

questions.solution_text:
The graph is a downward-opening parabola with its highest point at $(0,8)$.
Check the point $(2,6)$: $y=-\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}+8=-2+8=6$.
The equation is $y=-\frac{1}{2}x^{2}+8$; it also gives $y=0$ at $x=4$.
